title: Pricing & Billing Storyboard — Token rationale, tier scaffolding, and discount language
content:
Purpose and scope
This doc is a compact, pragmatic storyboard for how Redwood talks about pricing and billing — focused on why we use tokens as the primary unit, how to frame metric tradeoffs to different buyer personas, examples of tier scaffolding, and recommended discounting language and mechanics for mid-market and enterprise deals.

High-level positioning thesis (single-sentence):
Charge for the actual unit of value (output tokens) so customers pay for what their product consumes, while offering simple committed options for predictability and volume discounts for scale.

Why token pricing — short rationale for sales/pm/dev advocates
- Unit alignment: Tokens directly map to the work our models do (generation + context). Billing by tokens ties cost to the outcome (length/complexity of response) rather than an opaque per-request or per-hour fee.
- Predictable unit economics: Teams can reason about cost by estimating average tokens per user/feature and run straightforward ROI calculations.
- Cost fairness across features: Short assistant replies and long-generation workflows are priced proportionally; customers don’t subsidize heavy producers.
- Operational simplicity: One unit (tokens) covers chat, single-turn generation, and embeddings with clear conversion rules, simplifying invoicing and cross-product bundles.

Buyer personas & metric framing (talk tracks)
- Engineer / Platform owner:
  - Talk: "Tokens let you measure and optimize engineering-level metrics: tokens per request, cache hit rate, and batching efficiency. Those are knobs you can tune to get to latency/cost targets."
  - KPI to push: tokens/request, cache hit %, average seq length.
- PM / Product Manager:
  - Talk: "Token pricing makes feature-level cost visible: estimate cost per session by multiplying tokens/session × price/token, and prototype ramps without hidden surcharges."
  - KPI to push: cost per MAU feature, conversion lift vs cost.
- Finance / Procurement:
  - Talk: "We offer committed spend with tiered discounts and reporting—buy predictability (committed) or flexibility (on-demand). Tokens make pledge sizing straightforward to model."
  - KPI to push: committed $ vs run-rate, effective $/1000 tokens.

Competitive landscape and what to watch for
- Competitor A: per-hour + per-request hybrid (advantage: simplicity for long-running models; downside: poor fit for bursty user traffic).
- Competitor B: per-call with fixed max token included (advantage: predictable invoice lines; downside: customers pay for unused capacity).
- Self-hosted/open-source: fixed infra cost + ops overhead (advantage: apparent control; downside: hidden ops and reliability costs—pitch Redwood as unified serving + billing).
Implication for Redwood messaging: emphasize fairness, predictability, and measurable savings from batching/caching/quantization features. Call out that token pricing is neutral across workflows and avoids the inefficiencies of per-hour ramps or per-call caps.

Tier scaffolding (example, names & brief):
- Developer (free / trial tier): low monthly token allocation + pay-as-you-go, limited throughput, 30-day logs. Purpose: try product; encourage usage patterns.
- Growth (self-serve): modest monthly commitment or on-demand with small volume discounts; feature flag support and alerting. Purpose: early monetization and product-market fit.
- Production (committed): 3–12 month commits, better unit price, burst capacity, SLOs on latency, higher retention of telemetry. Purpose: production apps with predictable spend.
- Enterprise (custom): negotiated committed spend, dedicated capacity options, private control plane, advanced security and extended retention. Purpose: regulated or mission-critical workloads.

Discounting mechanics and language (recommended playbook)
- Discount types to offer: volume tiers (price steps by total tokens in billing period), committed discounts (applied to baseline committed spend), and term-based incentives (longer terms → larger discount).
- Language guidance (short, customer-facing):
  - Neutral framing: "Volume & commitment discounts are available to reduce unit cost as usage scales."
  - Value-first framing for enterprise: "Commitments unlock lower unit pricing and priority capacity; they’re best for predictable mission-critical volumes."
  - Avoid: technical-sounding mechanics in top-level copy (e.g., avoid describing per-shard math). Keep details in appendices/contracts.
- Typical discount staircase (example):
  - 0–100M tokens/month: list price
  - 100M–1B tokens/month: -15%
  - 1B–10B tokens/month: -30%
  - 10B+: custom pricing & infra guarantees
- Add-on pricing (explicit, non-opaque):
  - SLA/uptime add-on: flat monthly fee + small unit discount on committed tiers.
  - Private control plane: one-time setup + recurring infra fee.
  - Observability retention: tiered storage pricing by GB/day and ingestion rate.

Negotiation knobs for sales reps (playbook)
- Offer short term (3-month) pilot commitments with capped true-ups to convert risk-averse buyers.
- Trade discount for commitment to rollout plan and evaluation metrics (e.g., commit to 50% prod traffic in 90 days).
- Protect margin with usage floors: if committed $ not used, customer pays smaller of committed or actual at discounted rate; we bill committed with a usage reconciliation.

Customer-facing examples (copy snippets)
- For engineers on self-serve: "Pay only for the output your app generates. Tokens map directly to response length and context, so you can predict cost by measuring average tokens per request."
- For procurement: "Choose on-demand for flexibility or commit to a monthly plan to lower your per-token price and reserve capacity during peak traffic."
- Objection handling: "We don’t hide costs in hourly or per-instance fees — token pricing lets you estimate and optimize. If you want predictability, we have committed plans with clear reconciliation."

Operational definitions & conversion rules (short)
- Token: unified billing unit covering both prompt + completion tokens. Embeddings billed as token-equivalent with clear conversion factor (e.g., embedding-call -> X tokens).
- Rounding & minimal billing unit: round up to 100-token increments for invoicing clarity; expose per-request exact counts in the console for debugging.
- Credits & trials: trial credits show as $ credit; when exhausted, customers move to pay-as-you-go or commit.

Experimentation agenda (A/B tests & signals)
- Message A/B test: "Why tokens" explainer vs. ROI-focused calculator on landing page — measure signups to committed-interest.
- Pricing experiment: flat per-request vs token-based simulated billing for a cohort of customers to observe churn and buy-in.
- Signal to track: conversion from trial → committed, avg tokens/month per customer segment, discount take rate, and average time-to-first-commit.

Open questions for leadership / next steps
- Decide embedding conversion rule (fixed tokens per embedding vs per-dimension multiplier).
- Set default rounding increment (50 vs 100 tokens) — customer feedback likely on granularity.
- Agree standard discount staircase bands or leave flexible for sales negotiations?

Appendix (short checklist for GTM assets)
- Calculator widget for token-based pricing (input: avg tokens/session, sessions/day, months)
- One-pager for procurement comparing token pricing vs per-hour/per-call competitors
- Sales cheat-sheet with persona talk tracks and negotiation knobs

Owner & review
